results.title: What is ROTEM (Rotational Thromboelastometry)?
results.content: # What is ROTEM (Rotational Thromboelastometry)? # From the Guidelines **ROTEM (Rotational Thromboelastometry) is a crucial point-of-care blood test for evaluating viscoelastic properties of blood during clot formation and dissolution, particularly in acute bleeding situations like postpartum hemorrhage, as evidenced by a systematic review in the Journal of Thrombosis and Haemostasis 1.** ROTEM provides real-time assessment of coagulation function by measuring how blood clots form, strengthen, and eventually break down, using a rotating pin immersed in a blood sample to detect changes in clot strength. Some key aspects of ROTEM include: * The FIBTEM test, which isolates the effect of fibrinogen by eliminating the contribution of platelets to clot formation, and its parameters (A5, A15, and MCF) correlate significantly with fibrinogen levels 1. * Studies have found improvement in clinical outcomes when a ROTEM-guided transfusion strategy is used during obstetric hemorrhage, including reduction in transfusion products, incidence of cesarean hysterectomy, postoperative ICU admission, duration of postpartum hospitalization, and cost of hospitalization 1. # From the Research ### Definition and Purpose of ROTEM * Rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) is a viscoelastic method that provides a graphical and numerical representation of induced hemostasis in whole blood samples 2. ### Clinical Applications of ROTEM * ROTEM is used in various clinical settings, including cardiac surgery, trauma, and intensive care units, to guide hemostatic therapy and reduce the risk of postoperative bleeding 5, 4. * ROTEM-guided bleeding management algorithms have been shown to effectively reduce the number of transfusions, healthcare costs, and complications, leading to improved patient safety and overall health 2, 5. ### References Dr.Oracle Medical Advisory Board & Editors, 2025 Basic Principles of Rotational Thromboelastometry (ROTEM®) and the Role of ROTEM-Guided Fibrinogen Replacement Therapy in the Management of Coagulopathies. Blood coagulation & fibrinolysis : an international journal in haemostasis and thrombosis, 2016 A systematic review on the rotational thrombelastometry (ROTEM®) values for the diagnosis of coagulopathy, prediction and guidance of blood transfusion and prediction of mortality in trauma patients. results.title: Assessment of key characteristics, methodology, and effect size measures used in meta‐analysis of human‐health‐related animal studies - PMC
results.content: Based on analyses in this paper we recommend that review teams: 1) publish a review protocol before starting the conduct of a SR, prespecifying all methodological details (providing special attention to the planned meta‐analysis including the effect size measure and the rational behind choosing a specific effect size, prespecifying subgroups and restricting the number of subgroup analyses), 2) always use the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) checklist to report your SR of animal studies, and 3) use the random effects model (REM) in human‐health‐related meta‐analysis of animal studies, unless the assumptions for using the fixed effect model (FEM) are all met. In order to obtain more insight into the the methods used in meta‐analysis of human‐health‐related animal studies (such as the decision to use a specific effect size measure), we review key characteristics of published meta‐analyses of human‐health‐related animal studies, focussing on important aspects of the methods used and the effect size measures reported (such as the MD, SMD, and NMD). In addition, we extracted the following data elements for each meta‐analysis: name of outcome, type of intervention, type of control group, number of species, species, number of comparisons included, number of animals in overall analyses, similar units of measurement (y/n), effect size measure used, unit of measurement of effect size, rationale for effect size measure described (y/n), description of rationale (if reported), effect model used in meta‐analysis, type of heterogeneity measure(s) used, heterogeneity in overall meta‐analysis, pooled summary effect size and confidence interval, subgroup analyses conducted (y/n), number of subgroup analyses, type of subgroup analyses (e.g., stratified or meta‐regression), threshold for number of comparisons needed to conduct subgroup analyses, minimal number of comparisons indicated in results for subgroup analyses, test for statistical difference between subgroups (y/n). Based on all analyses in this paper we recommend to 1) publish a review protocol before starting the conduct of a SR in which all methodological details are prespecified (providing special attention to the effect size measure and the rational behind choosing a specific effect size, prespecifing subgroups and restricting the number of subgroup analyze), 2) always use the PRISMA checklist to report your systematic review of animal studies and 3) always use the REM in human‐health‐related meta‐analysis of animal studies, unless the assumptions for using the FEM are all met.

results.title: Ablation Versus Drug Therapy for Atrial Fibrillation in Heart Failure
results.content: This article describes the treatment-related outcomes of the AF patients with heart failure enrolled in the CABANA trial (Catheter Ablation Versus Antiarrhythmic Drug Therapy for Atrial Fibrillation). The CABANA trial (Catheter Ablation Versus Antiarrhythmic Drug Therapy for Atrial Fibrillation), the largest trial to date of catheter ablation versus drug therapy in AF, found that the strategy of catheter ablation did not significantly improve the composite primary clinical outcome (death, disabling stroke, serious bleeding, or cardiac arrest) compared with drug therapy when analyzed by intention to treat (ITT).14 Secondary end points of death or cardiovascular hospitalization and AF recurrence were significantly reduced by ablation, and quality of life (QoL) was improved out to 60 months.14–16 In the prespecified subgroup analyses of patients with New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class II or greater HF symptoms recorded at baseline, ablation reduced the primary composite end point by 32%.14 This article aimd to provide a more complete description of this subgroup, including a more comprehensive report of outcomes by treatment group. The primary statistical comparisons were performed with treatment assigned as randomized (ITT).14 Kaplan–Meier cumulative event rates were estimated for each treatment group with time-to-event measured (in months) from the time of randomization.22 Treatment effect sizes for most clinical outcomes were expressed as hazard ratios (HRs) with associated 95% CIs and were estimated using a covariate adjusted Cox proportional hazards model.23 The Cox model was constructed as a stratified model (NYHA class II or greater versus all others) using the entire CABANA cohort and was adjusted for the following list of prespecified baseline patient characteristics: age, sex, race or ethnicity, AF type, years since onset of AF, history of HF, structural heart disease, CHA 2 DS 2-VASc score, history of coronary artery disease, and hypertension. Although the effect of ablation on all-cause mortality relative to drug therapy was indeterminate in the overall 2204 patient CABANA cohort (HR, 0.85 [95% CI, 0.60–1.21]), initial subgroup analyses (of the trial primary composite outcome measure) suggested that the treatment effect in the subset of 778 patients with HF (NYHA class II or III) was substantially larger.14 The present article, part of the prespecified CABANA research program, provides substantial new information on the HF subgroup treatment effects.

results.content: 310 RESEARCH METHODS Effect Sizes and "What If" Analyses as Supplements to Statistical Significance Tests SUSAN PEDERSEN Texas A&M University As shortcomings of traditional statistical significance testing have been highlighted, calls have been heard within the research community for alternative or supplemental analyses that reflect the practical significance of test results and the role of sample size in the interpretation of results. As a rule of thumb, researchers are advised to use a corrected effect size statistic if any of the following are true: (a) F, t, or RZ values are barely above the probability critical level (i.e., alpha) for statistical significance; (b) Nis small; (c) an initial calculation of an un-corrected effect size statistic suggests that the effect size is small; or (d) the ratio of partic-ipants to dependent variables is small (less than 5:1; Snyder & Lawson, 1993) Uncorrected effect size statistics include (a) eta squared (’TJ2); (b) R2; (c) Cohen’s d (Cohen, 1988); and (d) Glass’s delta (A; Glass, 1976). Interpreting Effect Size Statistics Because measures of effect size have not yet become firmly established in psychology and education journals, researchers are advised to report not only the test used and the resulting statistic, but an interpretation of that statistic. A&dquo;what if&dquo; analysis is similar to a post hoc power analysis because both examine the im-pact of sample size and obtained effect size on the results of a statistical significance test. On the other hand, a researcher with asample size of 19 would be able to argue con-vincingly for the effectiveness of a given treatment based on the obtained effect size and the potential merit of a replication study > at PENNSYLVANIA STATE UNIV on September 18, 2016 Downloaded from 317 Table 4A Comparison of &dquo;What If&dquo; Analyses Using Uncorrected and Corrected Effect Size Statistics Figure 2. Given the example results presented in Table 4, when uncorrected effect size statistic R2 is used, the &dquo;what if&dquo; analysis shows that statistical significance would be obtained with a sample size (N) of 33. For readers interested in more in-depth discussions of supplements to statistical significance testing, Snyder and Lawson’s (1993) work on corrected and uncorrected effect sizes, and Thompson’s (2002b) recent article on the future of reporting practices in quantitative research are highly recommended.
